In addition, new research will look laterally at the state of AV deployment in areas such as freight and goods movement and package and food delivery. These assessments will use the U.S. Department of Energy’s technology maturity and market readiness assessment scales for comparison. • AV fleet operations management. Phase III revealed the complexity of the various subsystems needed for AV fleet operations with respect to electrification and station operations. Phase IV is beginning to delve further into AV fleet management functions, including emerging business models and operational protocols involved in managing AV technology for public mobility applications. This includes the numerous subsystems, facilities, communications, and human/machine interfaces that comprise the operations management supporting the AV fleet(s) within the urban environment. • New mobility systems simulation. Phase III identified the need for a SEM for the planning, analysis, and operation of the multiple modes and subsystems of an AMD, often referred to as a “digital twin.” Most existing simulation tools allow effective analysis of traditional modes of travel but are challenged when applied to model emerging modes and to encompass simulations of multimodal travel. As an extension of the SEM, future work will identify available simulation tools and assess gaps in 55 This report is available at no cost from the National Laboratory of the Rockies at www.nlr.gov/publications. capability to support the SEM process, particularly for AV and other emerging mobility technology in combination with traditional modes, microtransit, and nonmotorized forms of travel. • Critical information exchange. Early deployments are exposing the importance of coordination of critical information exchange between infrastructure owners and operators and AV fleets in areas pertaining to emergency response, roadway network impacts (e.g., construction, detours, maintenance), and special events. This is typically network-level information beyond the sensor range of any individual vehicle. Such information reflects events and circumstances such as floods, major roadway construction zones, and emergency response (e.g., fires, active shooters). This research is being coordinated with the U.S. Department of Transportation’s Center for Excellence on New Mobility and Automated Vehicles, building on the initial research by NLR entitled Data for Autonomous Transportation Awareness: Data Exchange Use Cases, Standards, and Barriers (Young, Fish, and Mir 2026). • Human response to unattended, driverless vehicles. Many AV applications in which multiple parties share a vehicle have had an attendant on board, ostensibly to assist the vehicle when needed, but the attendant also serves another purpose as an authority and moderator among passengers. People are accustomed to riding in elevators with others, but those rides tend to be short—and behavior and norms in an elevator have been standardized for much of the past century. In the case of AV operations, where trips are of longer duration and without established norms, much remains unknown about how people might interact in the absence of an attendant.
